explain.say: The cochlea is a snail-shaped tube full of fluid. Running along it is a strip called the basilar membrane, lined with thousands of hair cells that turn movement into nerve signals.

explain.say: The strip is narrow and stiff at the start and wide and floppy at the far end. High notes shake the start and low notes travel to the tip, so the brain knows pitch from which hair cells fire.

faq.a: The cochlea is the hearing organ of the inner ear. It turns vibrations in its fluid into nerve signals, sorting them by pitch along its length.
asks: What is the snail shape in the ear?

faq.q: How does the ear tell high and low sounds apart?
faq.a: Each part of the basilar membrane in the cochlea vibrates most at one pitch: high pitches near the base, low pitches near the tip. The brain works out the pitch from which hair cells are active.
asks: How does the ear know a high note?

faq.a: Hair cells are sensory cells in the cochlea topped with tiny bristles. When fluid movement bends the bristles, the cell sends an electrical signal to the hearing nerve. Each ear has roughly 15,000 of them.
asks: What do hair cells in the ear do?
How many hair cells are in the ear?

faq.a: The ossicles, called the hammer, anvil and stirrup, are the three smallest bones in the body. They carry vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea and concentrate them, boosting the pressure about twenty times.
asks: What are the three tiny bones in the ear?

faq.q: What is the range of human hearing?
faq.a: Young people can hear from about 20 vibrations a second, a deep rumble, up to about 20,000 a second, a thin whine. The top of the range usually drops as people get older.

facts: Humans typically hear sounds from about 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz.
The stirrup, or stapes, in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the human body.
High-pitched sounds are detected near the base of the cochlea and low-pitched sounds near its tip.
